challenges.name: fix-the-flaky-pipeline-evidence
challenges.title: Fix the Flaky Pipeline: read the evidence
challenges.description: The test workflow of the CodeDev API goes red about one run in five and a re-run of the same commit is green. Six statements on one evidence pack - the CI history (A), two failure logs (B, C), the code and tests involved (D) and a pull request that adds retries (E) - take you from reading the evidence to a hypothesis, past a tempting wrong fix, to a real fix and how to prove it.

questions.question:
Evidence A - CI history, workflow "test" on main (vitest run), last 8 of 50 runs:
Run    Commit   Started (UTC)        Duration  Result  Failed test
#1849  9d03b7e  2026-10-26 08:41:12  2m 38s    pass    (re-run of #1848)
#1848  9d03b7e  2026-10-26 08:37:55  2m 41s    FAIL    leaderboard.test.ts > ranks learners by points, ties by name
#1847  c51a2f0  2026-10-26 07:58:20  2m 44s    pass
#1846  4e1c9a2  2026-10-26 07:12:03  2m 40s    pass    (re-run of #1845)
#1845  4e1c9a2  2026-10-26 07:08:19  2m 39s    FAIL    enrollment.test.ts > trial ends 7 days after enrolment
#1844  b7710de  2026-10-25 16:20:47  2m 42s    pass
#1843  0aa93f1  2026-10-25 14:55:09  2m 40s    pass
#1842  0aa93f1  2026-10-25 14:31:26  2m 43s    pass
Last 50 runs: 40 pass, 10 FAIL (6 x enrollment.test.ts, 4 x leaderboard.test.ts).
Every failed commit passed on a re-run. Median duration: pass 2m 41s, FAIL 2m 40s.

Statement: "Commits 4e1c9a2 and 9d03b7e each failed and then passed with exactly the same code, so the result depends on something that changes from run to run - such as the time a test runs at, the order the tests run in, or state left behind by another test - and not on the code alone."
questions.explanation: True. A re-run uses the same commit, the same dependencies and the same tests, yet the result flips, so the outcome depends on an input that is not in the code: the clock, the order of the tests, state shared between tests, randomness, or the network. The history also argues against the usual first suspect, a slow CI machine: failed runs take the same time as passing ones (median 2m 40s against 2m 41s). The misconception is to treat "passed on re-run" as "nothing is wrong"; it is the definition of a flaky test, and each failure is a real outcome that happens with some probability.

True. The test computes its expected value first, then spends about 150 ms creating a course, then calls enrollInTrial, which reads the clock again. Both round down to the whole second. If both reads fall in the same second (07:09:40.2 and 07:09:40.35) the values match; if the second ticks over in between (07:09:40.9 and 07:09:41.05) the code rounds to 07:09:41 and the test expected 07:09:40 - exactly one second, as in log B. With 150 ms between the reads, roughly one run in seven crosses a second, which fits 6 failures in 50 runs. The misconception is that two Date.now() calls in one test see the same time; the fix is to give the code a clock the test controls.

False. On its own, the test starts with an empty map and inserts an, binh, chi in that order. The comparator only compares points, and Array.prototype.sort is stable, so the tie between an and binh keeps insertion order and the test passes every time. It fails only when streak.test.ts ran earlier in the same worker: with isolate: false the module, and its map, is shared between files, so binh is already in the map and setPoints("binh", 120) keeps binh's earlier position. Which files share a worker, and in which order, changes between CI runs. Two lessons hide here: shared module state makes the result depend on order, and the code never implemented "ties by name" at all - the test passed by luck of insertion order. The misconception is that a test which passes alone is correct.

questions.question:
Evidence E - PR #611 "ci: retry flaky tests 3 times":
 export default defineConfig({
   test: {
     isolate: false,
+    retry: 3, // flaky tests: try again up to 3 times before failing the build
   },
 });

Evidence A - CI history, workflow "test" on main (vitest run), last 8 of 50 runs:
Run    Commit   Started (UTC)        Duration  Result  Failed test
#1849  9d03b7e  2026-10-26 08:41:12  2m 38s    pass    (re-run of #1848)
#1848  9d03b7e  2026-10-26 08:37:55  2m 41s    FAIL    leaderboard.test.ts > ranks learners by points, ties by name
#1847  c51a2f0  2026-10-26 07:58:20  2m 44s    pass
#1846  4e1c9a2  2026-10-26 07:12:03  2m 40s    pass    (re-run of #1845)
#1845  4e1c9a2  2026-10-26 07:08:19  2m 39s    FAIL    enrollment.test.ts > trial ends 7 days after enrolment
#1844  b7710de  2026-10-25 16:20:47  2m 42s    pass
#1843  0aa93f1  2026-10-25 14:55:09  2m 40s    pass
#1842  0aa93f1  2026-10-25 14:31:26  2m 43s    pass
Last 50 runs: 40 pass, 10 FAIL (6 x enrollment.test.ts, 4 x leaderboard.test.ts).
Every failed commit passed on a re-run. Median duration: pass 2m 41s, FAIL 2m 40s.

Statement: "Merging PR #611 fixes the pipeline: a test that fails and then passes on a retry has shown that the code works."
questions.explanation: False. A retry runs the same test again until the dice come up right; it changes how often the build is red, not why. The leaderboard test is pointing at a real bug - production ranks tied learners by insertion order, not by name - and with three retries it would almost always go green and hide it. The enrolment test would keep failing about one run in seven and pass on the retry, so every future timing bug in that file would be hidden too. Retries can be acceptable for a short time on tests that cross a real network, with a ticket to remove them; for unit tests that depend on the clock and on order they only remove the signal. The misconception is that a green retry is evidence; it is a second sample of a random result.

True. Each change removes one source of nondeterminism instead of hiding it. With an injected clock the test and the code see the same instant, so there is no second to cross. An explicit tie-breaker makes the order a rule of the code ("ties by name", as the test name says) instead of an accident of which test inserted a user first. A fresh leaderboard per test removes the dependency on other files, so isolate: false can stay for speed. The misconception is that the fix belongs only in the tests: two of the three changes are in the production code, because the tests had found real problems in it.

Statement: "After the fix, five passing CI runs in a row show that the flakiness is gone."
questions.explanation: False. Before the fix the pipeline already passed 4 runs in 5, so five green runs in a row happen with probability 0.8^5, about 33%, on code that is still broken - and the default file order may never put streak.test.ts before leaderboard.test.ts. Useful evidence forces the conditions that caused the failures: run the suite many times (for example 100) with a shuffled order and a different seed each time, and pin the clock to the edge of a second (07:09:40.999) in a test. A broken pipeline passes 100 runs with probability 0.8^100, about 2 in 10 billion. The misconception is that a few green runs prove the absence of a random failure.

challenges.name: fix-the-flaky-pipeline
challenges.title: Fix the Flaky Pipeline
challenges.description: The CodeDev trial week module keeps a small leaderboard for learners on a 7-day trial and tells them when the trial ends. Its tests go red about one CI run in five: sometimes the trial end is wrong, sometimes the ranking comes back in a different order, and a re-run of the same code is green. Locally, one test at a time, everything passes. Fix startCohort(now) so that every cohort gives the same answer for the same start time and awards, whatever order the awards arrive in and whatever ran before: trialEndsAt() is 7 days after the moment the cohort started (the time the injected clock now() returned when startCohort ran), rounded down to the whole second, as an ISO string; ranking() lists every learner with points as "name points", most points first, ties in alphabetical order of name; and every cohort starts empty. Awards whose points are not a positive whole number are ignored (that part already works). Input (read by the test runner, do not change it): { runs, seed, starts, awards }. Run i starts a cohort with a clock fixed at starts[i % starts.length] and gives it the awards in an order shuffled by a seeded random generator, so the shuffles are the same on every submission. Output: the number of runs and the seed, then every different ranking and, per start time, every different trial end, each with the number of runs that gave it. A correct module prints exactly one ranking line and one trial line per start time.
hints: Run the starter on the first public test and read the output: which parts of the answer change from run to run, and which inputs does the code read that the test runner does not control?

Look at three lines: where the map of points is created (once for the file, or once per cohort?), what trialEndsAt() reads instead of the `now` it was given, and whether ranking() decides the order of tied learners or leaves it to the order the awards arrived in.

A similar case: `const seen = new Set<string>(); function createInbox(clock: () => number) { return { add(id: string) { seen.add(id); }, list: () => [...seen], receivedAt: () => Date.now() }; }`. Two inboxes share `seen`, `list()` follows arrival order and `receivedAt()` ignores the clock. Moving `seen` inside createInbox, sorting in list() and calling clock() makes every inbox independent and repeatable.
